title: ARE WE PREACHING THE GOSPEL… OR JUST TELLING PEOPLE WHAT THEY WANT TO HEAR?
paragraphs: ARE WE PREACHING THE GOSPEL… OR JUST TELLING PEOPLE WHAT THEY WANT TO HEAR?
When the Church Becomes Afraid to Offend, the Cross Becomes Easy to Ignore—and Souls Are Left Comforted in the Very Things Jesus Came to Save Them From.
What if the most dangerous sermon you ever heard was the one that made you feel wonderful about yourself… but never brought you face-to-face with the truth about your soul?

What if you walked into church carrying secret sin, hidden bitterness, an unforgiving heart, a life slowly drifting away from God… and walked out smiling because someone told you that your breakthrough was coming?
You were encouraged.
You were celebrated.
You were told you were chosen, favored, blessed, destined for greatness.
But nobody told you to repent.
Nobody spoke about the holiness of God.
Nobody explained why Jesus had to bleed on a cross.
And nobody loved you enough to ask whether you had truly surrendered your life to Christ.
You went home feeling better.
But were you any closer to Jesus?
That question should trouble every preacher, every Christian content creator, every ministry leader, and every believer who has ever confused making people feel good with helping people become holy.
Because there is a terrifying possibility we need to confront.
We can fill churches with people who love hearing about Jesus while never teaching them what it means to follow Him.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is that some of those people are not deliberately rejecting the Gospel.
They have simply never heard it clearly.
They have heard about blessings without surrender.
Favor without faithfulness.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Heaven without the narrow gate.
A crown without a cross.
And a Savior who supposedly exists to fulfill their dreams rather than a King who calls them to lay down their lives.

Somewhere along the way, we must ask ourselves whether we have been faithfully proclaiming the Gospel of Jesus Christ or gradually replacing it with a message that people are more comfortable consuming.
Because the difference is not small.
It is eternal.
The apostle Paul warned Timothy about precisely this danger.
In 2 Timothy 4:3–4, he wrote:

“For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.” (KJV)
There is something painfully recognizable about those words.
Paul did not merely warn that people would stop listening to religious teaching.
He warned that people would actively seek teachers who would tell them what they wanted to hear.

The Greek expression translated “itching ears” includes the participle κνηθόμενοι (knēthomenoi), from a verb meaning to itch or tickle. It creates a vivid picture of listeners whose desires shape the kind of teaching they seek.
They are not necessarily looking for the truth that will correct them.
They are looking for words that will satisfy them.
And before we point toward some famous preacher, some enormous congregation, or some viral Christian influencer, we need to confront a more uncomfortable possibility.
Sometimes those itching ears belong to us.
Sometimes we want a sermon about God's promises but become restless when the preacher talks about our pride.
We rejoice when someone tells us that God has a purpose for our lives, but become defensive when Scripture confronts our sexual immorality, dishonesty, greed, unforgiveness, or hypocrisy.
We love hearing that God knows our hearts.
But we become uncomfortable when Jeremiah 17:9 reminds us that the human heart is deceitful and desperately sick.
We want Jesus to heal our wounds.
But do we want Him to expose the sins we have been protecting?
We want Him to restore our peace.
But will we allow Him to interrupt our rebellion?
We want resurrection power.
But we do not always want to die to ourselves.
And that is where the question becomes deeply personal.
Do we love Jesus for who He truly is, or have we become attached to a version of Him who never disagrees with us?
Imagine a man sitting in the back row of a church.
He has not been faithful to his wife.
He has lied to people who trust him.
His private life is collapsing beneath the weight of decisions nobody knows about.
He is exhausted from pretending.
But something inside him still hopes God has not abandoned him.
He enters the sanctuary carrying guilt he cannot explain.
The preacher begins speaking.
“You are about to enter your season of increase!”
The congregation erupts.
“Your enemies are about to watch God elevate you!”
People stand and applaud.
“Nothing can stop what God has prepared for you!”
The man joins the applause.
For a moment, he feels hope.
But his conscience is still crying out.
What about my wife?
What about the lies?
What about the person I have become?
What about the sin I cannot seem to escape?
What about Jesus?
And the service ends.
He leaves with a promise of promotion, but without hearing the call to repentance that his soul desperately needed.
Now imagine something different.
The preacher opens the Bible and speaks about David.
A man who had known God's favor.
A man who had worshiped sincerely.
A man who had nevertheless committed adultery, arranged a death, and attempted to conceal his guilt.
Then the preacher explains how the prophet Nathan confronted David.
Not to entertain him.
Not to humiliate him for an audience.
But to bring his hidden evil into the light.
And David finally confessed.
“I have sinned against the LORD.” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
The preacher does not stop with condemnation.
He speaks about the mercy of God.
He speaks about Psalm 51, where David pleads for cleansing and a renewed heart.
He explains that sin is serious, its consequences can be devastating, and forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence.
Then he speaks about Jesus Christ, the greater Son of David, who never sinned and who gave Himself to redeem sinners.
And the man in the back row begins to weep.
Not because somebody promised him a bigger house.
Not because somebody guaranteed him financial success.
But because, perhaps for the first time in years, he understands that he can stop hiding.
He must face the truth.
He must repent.
He must seek to make right what he has damaged wherever possible.
And he can come to Christ for mercy.
That sermon may not have made him comfortable.
But it may have been the sermon that pointed him toward life.
This is why biblical love cannot be reduced to making people feel affirmed.
A physician who refuses to tell a patient about a serious illness because the diagnosis might upset them is not demonstrating compassion.
And a preacher who deliberately conceals the reality of sin, judgment, repentance, and the cross to preserve an audience's approval is not necessarily protecting people.
They may be withholding the very truth those people need.
Yet we must be careful here.
The Gospel is not permission for preachers to become cruel.
It is not a justification for shouting at wounded people, publicly humiliating struggling believers, or treating every question as rebellion.
Jesus was full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And if our preaching has truth without compassion, we are not faithfully representing His heart.
If our preaching has compassion without truth, we are not faithfully representing His message.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners also called them to repentance.
The same Jesus who wept over Jerusalem also warned Jerusalem.
The same Jesus who forgave His enemies also spoke about judgment.
He did not soften the truth to win applause.
And He did not abandon love when the truth became painful.
Consider His encounter with the rich young ruler.
The man came asking about eternal life.
He was morally serious.
He had religious knowledge.
He appeared eager to do what was right.
And Mark 10:21 records something extraordinary before Jesus confronted his deepest attachment.
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him…”
Jesus loved him.
Then Jesus challenged him to surrender the wealth that had become an obstacle in his heart and to follow Him.
The man walked away sorrowful.
And Jesus did not chase after him with a revised message designed to preserve his approval.
He did not say, “Forget what I said. Just remain comfortable.”
He allowed the weight of the truth to stand.
Because genuine love does not require us to tell people whatever will keep them happy.
Sometimes love tells the truth even when that truth may cause someone to walk away.
But notice something equally important.
Jesus' command to that man was not a universal formula requiring every believer to sell every possession in exactly the same manner.
It exposed the particular allegiance competing with God in that man's life.
And that raises a question we cannot avoid.
What is competing with Jesus in yours?
Is it money?
A relationship?
A private addiction?
A reputation?
The fear of being rejected?
The desire to be admired?
Perhaps it is even the need to appear spiritually successful.
Sometimes the idol is not something obviously wicked.
Sometimes it is something good that has quietly become more important to us than obedience to Christ.
And the Gospel confronts that too.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus proclaimed:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)

The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), a present imperative from metanoeō, calling for repentance—a change of mind and heart that turns a person toward God and bears fruit in a changed life.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what we have done.
It is not purchasing forgiveness through tears.
It is not achieving sinless perfection before we can come to Jesus.
It is turning from sin toward God, trusting the Savior who alone can forgive and transform us.
And the command stands beside another essential command.
Believe the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not simply a program for moral improvement.
It is the announcement of what God has accomplished through Jesus Christ.
We were sinners who could not save ourselves.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And everyone who comes to Him in genuine faith receives the forgiveness and new life that human effort could never earn.
Paul summarizes this message in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures.
That is the center.
Not our success.
Not our comfort.
Not our popularity.
Not our influence.
Not our platform.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
If that message becomes secondary, something essential has been displaced.
A sermon can contain inspiring stories, emotional music, motivational language, and powerful personal testimonies.
Those things are not inherently wrong.
Encouragement is biblical.
Comfort is biblical.
Hope is biblical.
God's care for His children is biblical.
But none of these should replace the saving message of Christ.
We must not confuse a sermon that moves people emotionally with a sermon that faithfully explains God's Word.
Tears are not always repentance.
Applause is not always agreement with God.
A crowded altar is not automatically evidence of conversion.
And a viral message is not necessarily a faithful one.
At the same time, a small congregation is not automatically more faithful than a large one, and a difficult sermon is not automatically more biblical simply because people dislike it.
The measure is not how popular or unpopular the preacher becomes.
The measure is whether the message faithfully represents Scripture and directs people toward Christ.
Paul wrote in Galatians 1:10:
“For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.” (KJV)
Paul was not teaching that Christians should be unnecessarily offensive.
He was confronting the danger of compromising the Gospel to gain human approval.
There is a difference between speaking truth with gentleness and changing truth to avoid rejection.
And we need to recognize that difference before our desire to be accepted becomes stronger than our desire to be faithful.
This warning belongs not only to pastors.
It belongs to Christian writers.
To worship leaders.
To online ministries.
To Bible teachers.
To every person who posts Scripture on Facebook.
To us at Gospel Warrior.
Because it is possible to build an audience around Christian language while slowly becoming more concerned about audience reaction than biblical faithfulness.
We can begin measuring our effectiveness by the number of likes instead of the clarity of our witness.
We can become so afraid of losing followers that we avoid passages people desperately need to understand.
We can discover which words attract attention and gradually neglect the words that call people to surrender.
And when that happens, the danger is not merely that our content becomes shallow.
It is that our ministry begins serving the audience's preferences rather than the Lord's commission.
That is why every Christian platform, including this one, must remain accountable to Scripture.
You should never accept a message simply because Gospel Warrior published it.
Open your Bible.
Read the passage in context.
Examine the claims.
Ask whether the teaching points you toward Jesus or merely toward the personality delivering it.
The believers in Berea were commended in Acts 17:11 because they examined the Scriptures to determine whether the things they heard were true.
We need more of that spirit today.
Not suspicion for its own sake.
Not endless arguments over minor matters.
But humble, discerning love for God's Word.
And there is another side of this conversation that must not be ignored.
Some people have been deeply wounded by harsh religious environments.
They have heard sermons filled with condemnation but almost nothing about the mercy of Christ.
They have been made to feel that every struggle proves God despises them.
They have confused spiritual abuse with biblical correction.
If that describes your experience, please understand this.
The Gospel does not tell you to earn God's love through flawless performance.
It announces the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had successfully repaired ourselves.
Not after every sinful desire had disappeared.
Not after we had become impressive enough for heaven.
Christ died for sinners.
That truth is breathtaking.
And it is precisely why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is not a rival payment for salvation.
It is part of the response of faith to the God who saves by grace.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes the relationship clear.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are the fruit of God's transforming grace.
A changed life does not purchase the cross.
The cross makes a changed life possible.
So when a preacher calls you to repent, the biblical message should never be, “Make yourself worthy enough for Jesus.”
It should be, “Come to Jesus, because only He can save you.”
And when a preacher comforts a broken believer, the message should never be, “Your sin does not matter.”
It should be, “Your sin is serious, but the mercy of Christ is greater than your ability to save yourself.”
That is the beautiful tension of the Gospel.
It exposes us without leaving us hopeless.
It humbles us without declaring us worthless.
It confronts our rebellion while revealing the astonishing mercy of God.
It tells us that we cannot rescue ourselves.
And then it points us to the One who can.
Think about Peter.
He was confident.
Passionate.
Certain that he would remain loyal to Jesus.
Yet when the pressure came, he denied knowing his Lord three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memory of his own voice.
The realization that he had failed the very One he loved.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that after the rooster crowed, Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered His words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
We are not told everything Peter felt in that moment.
But we know what happened afterward.
The risen Jesus did not abandon Peter to his failure.
In John 21, He restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
Peter's denial was real.
His grief was real.
His restoration was real.
And Christ's grace did not merely make him feel better about denying Jesus.
It called him forward into renewed love and faithful service.
That is the difference between comforting someone in their sin and comforting someone with the Savior who can restore them.
One leaves the chains untouched.
The other points toward the One who breaks them.
And perhaps this is where your own story enters.
Maybe you have spent years appearing strong while secretly struggling.
Maybe you know exactly how to say “God is good” while your heart is filled with resentment.
Maybe you have learned to post Bible verses while avoiding the passage that confronts your own life.
Maybe you are a ministry worker who has become more concerned about maintaining an image than maintaining integrity.
Maybe you are a pastor who knows what Scripture says but fears what will happen if you preach it.
Maybe you are someone who stopped attending church because you were hurt, disappointed, or spiritually exhausted.
Or maybe you have never truly understood why Jesus died.
Wherever you find yourself, the invitation is not to become better at pretending.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Confession is not a performance designed to impress religious people.
It is agreeing with God about the truth.
No more defending what He calls sin.
No more disguising rebellion as personality.
No more using grace as an excuse to remain unchanged.
No more believing that shame must have the final word.
And no more running from the very Savior who came to rescue sinners.
The cross stands at the center of this invitation.
At Calvary, Jesus did not offer humanity a collection of motivational slogans.
He gave Himself.
The sinless Savior bore the suffering of the cross, died for our sins, and rose victorious.
He did not come merely to improve our self-image.
He came to reconcile us to God.
The Greek word καταλλαγή (katallagē), used in Romans 5:11 and 2 Corinthians 5:18–19, refers to reconciliation.
Through Christ, God brings those alienated by sin into a restored relationship with Himself.
This is more than feeling inspired.
More than enjoying religious content.
More than joining a community.
It is the miracle of being brought near to God through Jesus Christ.
And that reconciliation changes the way we understand everything.
Our identity.
Our priorities.
Our relationships.
Our money.
Our ambitions.
Our wounds.
Our future.
Even the way we preach.
Because once we understand the cost of our redemption, we can no longer treat the Gospel as a product to be adjusted according to consumer demand.
We are not authorized to edit away the cross because it makes people uncomfortable.
We are not authorized to remove repentance because it reduces applause.
And we are not authorized to promise material prosperity as though financial increase were the guaranteed evidence of God's favor.
Jesus Himself warned that following Him would involve self-denial and taking up the cross (Luke 9:23).
The apostles suffered.
Faithful Christians have experienced poverty, persecution, illness, grief, and loss.
Yet none of those hardships can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:35–39).
The Christian hope is not that every earthly difficulty will disappear.
It is that Christ has conquered sin and death, remains with His people, and will ultimately make all things new.
That hope is strong enough to sustain believers when easy promises fail.
It is strong enough for the hospital room.
The funeral.
The unemployment notice.
The broken marriage.
The lonely night.
The unanswered question.
The season when you pray and still have to wait.
The Gospel does not require us to deny suffering.
It gives us a Savior who entered suffering and overcame death.
And that is a message worth proclaiming even when it does not produce instant applause.
But now comes another uncomfortable question.
What happens when we, as believers, consume faithful biblical teaching but refuse to help carry it beyond ourselves?
We may share jokes, controversies, political arguments, advertisements, and countless pieces of entertainment without hesitation.
Yet sometimes we become strangely silent when something points people toward repentance, forgiveness, and eternal life.
We should never confuse a Facebook share with fulfilling the whole Great Commission.
Discipleship requires far more than clicking a button.
But sharing faithful Christian teaching can still be a meaningful act of witness.
A family member may be struggling with hidden guilt.
A friend may be drifting away from faith.
Someone you once worshiped with may be convinced that their failure has placed them beyond God's mercy.
A person who has never opened a Bible may be willing to read an article because it appeared on the profile of someone they trust.
You cannot control how another person responds.
You cannot force conviction.
You cannot manufacture conversion.
That work belongs to God.
But you can faithfully place truth where someone might encounter it.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Not to pressure anyone.
But because truth worth receiving is often worth passing on.
And think of one particular person who might benefit from it.
Not every spiritual struggle belongs in a public comment section.
Love knows the difference.
If you are reading this and something in your heart is being confronted, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
Not because a comment can save you.
Not because public confession is required to receive God's forgiveness.
But because sometimes writing a few sincere words helps us stop pretending that nothing is happening inside.
If you are weary from fighting the same spiritual battles, you can comment, “I'm still fighting.”
If you have been hiding behind religious appearances, you can write, “No more hiding.”
If you need prayer and are comfortable asking publicly, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if God has been restoring your life after a season of failure, consider sharing a testimony that points people toward Christ rather than toward yourself.
Your honesty may remind another struggling believer that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and restoration is not beyond the reach of God's grace.
We also need something deeper than occasional emotional moments online.
We need the steady nourishment of Scripture.
We need sound teaching.
Prayer.
Fellowship.
Accountability.
A faithful local church.
Believers who will encourage us when we are weak and lovingly correct us when we begin to wander.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior's desire to keep providing Christ-centered biblical content and discipleship resources.
These resources are intended to support personal study and spiritual growth, not replace Scripture itself or the life of a faithful local church.
And if you have been encouraged by this ministry, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Not because your salvation, spiritual standing, or God's approval can be purchased.
But it can be one meaningful way to give generously toward work you believe is faithful to the Gospel.
For some believers, this may be a fitting part of their planned charitable giving, alongside other responsibilities and commitments.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a transaction with heaven.
But gratitude, conviction, and willing participation in work intended to glorify Christ.
It is the opportunity to help make faithful biblical teaching and Christian resources accessible to others.
You are no less welcome here.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your thoughtful feedback matters.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
And your faithful walk with Jesus matters far more than any financial contribution.
If you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, you are warmly invited to join us for continuing Scripture-centered reflections, biblical encouragement, conviction, and discipleship.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who feels spiritually exhausted, the person wrestling with doubt, and even the person who does not yet believe in Jesus.
Not so we can build an audience around a ministry name.
But so more people might be encouraged to open the Scriptures, examine the truth, and encounter the message of Christ.
Because the goal was never supposed to be making Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Jesus known.
And that brings us back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Are we preaching the Gospel?
Or are we telling people what they want to hear?
The answer will not be found merely in how loudly we speak, how emotional our services become, how many followers we gain, or how confidently we quote Scripture.
It will be found in whether we faithfully proclaim the Christ revealed in the Bible.
The Christ who calls sinners to repentance.
The Christ who welcomes the weary.
The Christ who confronts hypocrisy.
The Christ who forgives the guilty.
The Christ who restores the fallen.
The Christ who died for our sins and rose again.
The Christ who is worthy of our trust, obedience, worship, and love.
And perhaps the most urgent question is not what every other preacher is saying.
Perhaps it is what we ourselves are willing to hear.
When Scripture corrects you, will you listen?
When Jesus calls you to surrender something you have been protecting, will you trust Him?
When the Gospel exposes the emptiness of your self-righteousness, will you cling to His grace instead?
When following Christ costs you approval, comfort, or convenience, will you still follow?
You do not need to pretend these are easy questions.
You do not need to manufacture an emotional answer.
You can begin with a simple, sincere prayer.

“Lord Jesus, show me where I have preferred comfortable words over Your truth. Forgive me for the ways I have resisted Your correction. Teach me to love Your Word, trust Your grace, turn from my sin, and follow You faithfully. Keep my heart tender toward the people You call me to love. Let my life point toward You. Amen.”
And if you have never truly placed your faith in Christ, do not mistake reading this article for receiving Him.
Turn to Him.
Believe the Gospel.
Call upon the Lord.
Seek to know Him through His Word.
Do not wait until you have become worthy.
Come because He is merciful.
If you are already His, return to the Scriptures with a willing heart.
Let the Gospel confront what needs to change.
Let grace strengthen what is weak.
Let truth expose what has been hidden.
And let the love of Christ shape the way you speak to others.
But above everything else, follow Jesus.
Because on the day we stand before Him, the greatest question will not be how many people applauded our message.
It will be whether we truly belonged to the Savior we claimed to proclaim.
The Gospel may wound our pride, but it never wounds us without pointing toward the mercy of Christ.
It may expose our sin, but it also reveals the Savior who died for sinners.
It may shatter the false stories we have told ourselves, but it gives us something infinitely better.
The truth.
And the truth is that no scandal is so great that the grace of Jesus is powerless to redeem the sinner who comes to Him in faith.
Peter's denial was not the end of his story.
David's failure did not place him beyond the possibility of repentance and mercy.
Paul's past as a persecutor did not prevent Christ from saving him and calling him into service.
And whatever has happened in your life, you do not need to write the final chapter without Jesus.
The Gospel is not the story of good people earning God's approval.
It is the story of a holy and merciful God saving sinners through His Son.
So let us preach it faithfully.
Let us receive it humbly.
Let us live it sincerely.
And let us never trade eternal truth for temporary applause.
Because the most heartbreaking tragedy is not that the truth made someone uncomfortable—it is that someone desperately needed the truth, and we were too afraid to tell them about Jesus.
